passages.title: A Shaded Route to School · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
The walk from Merdeka Street to Greenhill School is only six hundred metres, but students use it in different ways. The eastern side has a row of twelve young trees, three benches and a small drinking-water station near the bus stop. A painted line marks the part of the pavement where cyclists should slow down. In the morning, the trees provide shade for people waiting to cross the road. By midday, however, their shadows are shorter and the benches are warmer.

The school environmental club made a simple map of the route in June. It marked the shaded sections, the places where the pavement was uneven and two crossings that needed clearer signs. Club members also counted the number of people using the benches at three different times. They recorded an average of fourteen people during the morning period and six around midday. The count included adults and students, and it did not identify individual users.

The map is now displayed beside the school entrance. It helps new students choose a comfortable route and shows the local council where small improvements may be useful. The club has not measured road accidents or compared walking habits before and after the map was made. Its work describes the route and records how people used it during one month. It is a useful starting point, not proof that the street is now safe for every traveller.

passages.title: The School Repair Afternoon · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
Last Saturday, Greenhill School held its first repair afternoon in the covered sports area. The event began at nine o'clock, after student volunteers had moved six tables and placed signs near the entrance. Families were invited to bring small household items that could be checked safely. The school did not accept electrical devices with damaged wires or objects that needed specialist tools.

Twenty-six students joined the event. They worked at three stations: bags and clothing, bicycles, and simple wooden items. A local tailor showed students how to replace a loose button and repair a small tear. Two bicycle mechanics checked brakes and adjusted seats. At the final table, a teacher helped students tighten loose parts on wooden book stands. By noon, the volunteers had repaired eighteen items. Five other items were labelled and returned to their owners because they needed professional attention.

After the event, students wrote down what they had learned. Several said that asking an experienced person for advice was more useful than trying to fix everything quickly. The organisers counted repaired items, but they did not calculate how much money families saved or how long each repair lasted. The school plans to repeat the event next term and invite more volunteers. The first afternoon showed that practical cooperation can be enjoyable, although its long-term effect has not yet been measured.

passages.title: The Blue Notebook · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
When Rafi found a blue notebook under the last desk in the library, he first thought it belonged to a younger student. Its cover had a small drawing of a lighthouse, and several pages contained careful sketches of the sea. On the inside cover, someone had written, “For the person who notices what others leave behind.” There was no name or class number.

Rafi took the notebook to the librarian and asked her to send a general message to the class groups instead of naming anyone. She suggested placing it in the lost-property box, but Rafi hesitated. The sketches seemed too personal to leave among forgotten umbrellas and lunch containers. He remembered that a new student, Lila, often sat near the window and drew during breaks. He did not know whether the notebook was hers, so he avoided naming a possible owner.

The next morning, Lila came to the library. She recognised the lighthouse immediately, but she did not reach for the notebook until the librarian asked her to describe a page inside. Lila explained that the drawings were part of a project about her grandfather, who had worked near the coast. She thanked Rafi for not showing the pages to other students. Later, she added a note to the cover: “Thank you for returning the story, not just the book.” Rafi realised that careful actions can protect a person's privacy as well as return a lost object. He had wanted to solve a small problem, but he learned to think about how a solution might affect someone else.

passages.title: Testing a Classroom Water Filter Model · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
This classroom activity uses a simple filter model to show how visible particles can be separated from water. It is a demonstration, not a method for making unsafe water suitable for drinking. Students need a clear plastic bottle with its base removed by the teacher, clean cotton, a coffee filter, a container, and a small amount of soil mixed with tap water. The teacher should prepare the bottle before the lesson.

First, place the bottle upside down over the empty container. Put the coffee filter inside the neck and add a layer of clean cotton above it. Next, slowly pour a small cup of the soil mixture into the wide opening. Do not fill the bottle quickly, because the liquid may overflow. Wait until the water has passed through the layers. Observe the liquid in the container and compare it with a small sample of the original mixture. Students should record the colour and the amount of visible soil they can see.

Finally, remove the filter materials and place them in the waste bin. Wash the container and the work surface with the teacher's help. The filtered liquid must not be tasted or used for cooking. The model can trap some visible particles, but it does not remove every harmful substance or organism. In a science report, students should describe what they observed and avoid claiming that the demonstration produces drinking water.

passages.title: Why Schools Should Protect Quiet Spaces · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
A school should provide at least one quiet space where students can read, plan an assignment or take a short break between lessons. A quiet room does not need expensive furniture. A few tables, comfortable chairs, clear signs and agreed rules may be enough. The important point is that students have a place where conversation and movement are kept low.

There are several reasons to protect such spaces. First, students do not all learn in the same environment. Some can concentrate in a busy room, while others need fewer distractions to understand a long text. Second, a quiet area can support students who want to review notes before a test or read during a free period. Third, clear rules can help students share the room fairly. A timetable and a simple booking sheet may prevent one group from occupying it all day.

Some people argue that schools should use every available room for teaching or club activities. This concern is reasonable, especially when buildings are crowded. However, a quiet space can be shared at different times, and it may use an existing room rather than require a new building. Schools should ask students and teachers how often the space is needed before deciding its size. A short trial can show whether the arrangement is useful. The strongest argument is not that a quiet room will improve every student's grades, because that result has not been established. It is that a well-managed quiet space gives students another practical way to study and take responsibility for a shared resource.

passages.title: A Survey of Rooftop Gardens · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
A local education team reviewed rooftop gardens at three secondary schools over twelve weeks. Each school had a different garden size and a different number of student volunteers. The team recorded the number of active planting beds, the types of vegetables grown and the amount of water used each week. It also interviewed the teachers who supervised the gardens. The review focused on how the projects were organised, not on comparing students' academic results.

At the first school, volunteers maintained eight planting beds and grew spinach, tomatoes and spring onions. The second school had five beds and focused on herbs that could be used in cooking lessons. The third school had ten beds, but two were left empty during the school examination period because fewer volunteers were available. Across the three schools, teachers reported that a weekly duty list helped students remember watering and cleaning tasks. Water use was lower at the school that collected rainwater, although the team did not measure the cost of installing its storage tank.

The review found that garden routines were easier to maintain when tasks were shared and recorded. It did not prove that rooftop gardens improved science grades, reduced food costs or changed every student's eating habits. The schools also differed in roof design, sunlight and access to water, so their results cannot be compared as if the conditions were identical. The team recommended a longer review with the same measures at each school. Its findings describe early organisation and practical challenges; further evidence is needed before making wider claims about educational or environmental effects.
